anchor_text: fall to't yarely, or we run ourselves aground
summary: 'Yarely' means briskly, smartly, with ready skill — the nautical word for executing a maneuver without hesitation. The Master is telling the Boatswain to get the crew moving at once or the ship will be driven onto the rocks. It sets the urgent, practical register of the whole scene: on a ship in a storm, quick obedience is the only thing that matters.

The Boatswain echoes it twice a few lines later ('yare, yare!', TLN 6), turning it into the scene's rhythmic pulse of urgency. Its nautical specificity — along with 'topsail,' 'maincourse,' and 'lay her a-hold' — establishes the ship as a real working vessel before Prospero's magic is ever mentioned, so the storm reads as physically terrifying, not merely spectacular.

anchor_text: What cares these roarers for the name of king
summary: 'Roarers' is the Boatswain's word for the waves, whose noise 'roars' louder than any title. The question is rhetorical: the sea cares nothing for rank. The Boatswain is telling the King and his lords that on a sinking ship their social authority is worthless — only seamanship matters. Shakespeare makes this the scene's defining irony: the play's high-born rulers are helpless, and a blunt working sailor holds all the power.

The double sense sharpens the insult — the waves are the real bullies here, indifferent to the nobles' huffing. Onions (s.v. 'roarer') records the sense 'one who roars; bully, ruffian.' The leveling gesture — nature cares nothing for degree — is the scene's philosophical center and anticipates the play's broader questioning of authority and rank, from Gonzalo's ideal commonwealth to Caliban's dispossession.

anchor_text: he hath no drowning mark upon him: his complexion is perfect gallows
summary: Gonzalo is invoking the widespread proverb 'He that is born to be hanged shall never be drowned': a man with the 'gallows' written in his face — that is, a man destined to hang — cannot possibly drown, because fate has reserved a different death for him. The Boatswain's rough, bullying manner looks to Gonzalo like exactly the face of a man born for the noose, so Gonzalo takes comic comfort: as long as the Boatswain is alive on this ship, they cannot sink.

'Complexion' here means the outward appearance of character — the signs of a man's destiny supposedly readable in his face and manner, not merely his skin color. Gonzalo's speech is black comedy: he turns the Boatswain's insolence into evidence of an unfulfillable gallows-fate. The joke will return at 5.1 when Gonzalo recognizes the Boatswain on the miraculously restored ship and the proverb is wryly confirmed — the man who was born to hang did indeed survive the storm.

anchor_text: Bring her to try wi' th' maincourse
summary: 'Bring her to try' is the seamanship command to heave the ship almost head-on to the wind, letting it ride out a storm under minimal sail rather than trying to run before the gale. The 'maincourse' is the lowest and largest sail on the main mast — the only sail left set for exactly this maneuver. The Boatswain has just ordered the topsail taken in; now he is trying the last-resort tactic to keep the ship from being swamped.
detail: The technical precision here was recognizable to Elizabethan audiences who lived in a seafaring nation. 'Trying' (heaving-to) was the accepted response when a ship could neither run nor bear away in extreme weather; it is described in William Bourne's A Regiment for the Sea (1574), the standard English seamanship manual of the period. The Boatswain's commands in this scene are so accurate that scholars have used them to reconstruct the ship's situation: the topmast gone or stowed, the topsail furled, the ship now fighting to survive under the single maincourse sail. This nautical realism grounds the scene before Prospero's frame is revealed.

anchor_text: Out o' the moon, I do assure thee: I was the Man in the Moon, when time was

The episode is central to the scene's comic colonial dynamic: the newcomers are accepted as gods because they bring wine.

anchor_text: I'll show thee every fertile inch o' the island
summary: Caliban's offer to guide Stephano around the island and show him its resources — fresh springs, berries, nesting birds, pig-nuts, filbert nuts, scamels — exactly repeats what he did for Prospero when they first met, before the attempted rape of Miranda turned their relationship into master and slave (1.2). Montaigne's essay 'Of the Cannibals' had celebrated just this kind of natural generosity as 'uncorrupted' by civilization.

summary: Ferdinand opens with a compressed paradox: some sports (games, pastimes) are painful to perform, and the pleasure one takes in them 'sets off' the pain — that is, makes it look better by contrast, as a jewel is shown off against a dark background. Ferdinand is making a philosophical case for why he cheerfully hauls logs: the activity is 'odious' in itself but transformed by the mistress he serves, exactly as the pain of sport is transformed by the joy of playing.

anchor_text: Admir'd Miranda! / Indeed, the top of admiration
summary: Ferdinand plays on the Latin meaning of Miranda's name: from the Latin gerundive miranda, 'she who must be wondered at' or 'admirable one.' Ferdinand's pun is thus not merely wordplay but a small epiphany: he is the first outsider who meets her and discovers, aloud, the wonder inscribed in her name. The Tempest is uniquely a play about wonder (the word 'wonder' and its cognates appear more often here than in any other Shakespeare play), and Miranda embodies it before she speaks it.

anchor_text: all the more it seeks to hide itself, / The bigger bulk it shows. Hence, bashful cunning! / And prompt me, plain and holy innocence!
summary: Miranda coins a compressed paradox: the more her love tries to conceal itself (the 'trifling' of modesty), the more conspicuous it becomes — 'the bigger bulk it shows.' She then literally banishes that strategy with an apostrophe: 'Hence, bashful cunning!' — addressing her own disguising impulse as a thing to be sent away — and calls instead on 'plain and holy innocence' to speak for her. The rhetorical move enacts what it describes: she stops hiding and proposes marriage directly.
detail: The apostrophe ('Hence, bashful cunning!') is a figure of direct address to an abstraction; 'prompt me' continues it (innocence as a stage prompter). The paradox of concealment making something more visible was a commonplace of Renaissance love poetry and rhetoric; Shakespeare gives Miranda a tightly logical version of it. Her self-correction here — from strategy to directness — is the scene's moral turn: she is, of all the play's characters, the one most incapable of and unwilling to practice the 'cunning' the court world runs on.

anchor_text: A devil, a born devil, on whose nature Nurture can never stick; on whom my pains, Humanely taken, all, all lost, quite lost
summary: Prospero's soliloquy over Caliban is the play's sharpest statement of the nature-versus-nurture debate: Caliban's 'nature' (his inborn, inherited character) cannot be altered by 'nurture' (education, civilization, care). The effort to teach Caliban — language, knowledge, care — has been 'all lost.' This was the central question in Elizabethan and Jacobean colonial writing: could indigenous peoples be 'civilized' by European culture, or was their nature fixed?

Shakespeare leaves the question genuinely open: Prospero's anger may say more about the limits of his own approach (enslavement, not respect) than about any innate quality in Caliban. anchor_text: Now my charms are all o'erthrown, And what strength I have's mine own; Which is most faint
summary: The Epilogue breaks the dramatic frame: Prospero steps forward as the actor, not the character, and asks the audience directly for applause and release. Without his magic — and without the audience's goodwill — he is merely a man, trapped on the bare stage (the 'bare island'). The opening three lines establish the central reversal: all power is gone, and what remains is 'most faint.'

But this one is uniquely weighted: Prospero's entire play has been about the exercise of power; the Epilogue's first words strip it all away. The actor's hands, applauding, are the 'good hands' that will 'release' him — the pun on theatrical release (from the performance) and personal liberation fuses the play's themes of freedom and forgiveness with the theatrical event itself.

'Assaults Mercy' uses the siege-warfare metaphor that was conventional in Elizabethan devotional writing: prayer as a battering-ram at the gates of divine grace. The final couplet ('As you from crimes would pardon'd be, / Let your indulgence set me free') directly maps theatrical indulgence (the audience's charitable applause) onto doctrinal indulgence (the forgiveness of sins) — a pun that recasts theatre-going as a mutual act of grace.
